discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 precision

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping many neutral atoms at a 'magic wavelength' where the lattice light leaves the clock transition unperturbed, and demonstrated it experimentally. Ye developed the concept into the most precise clocks ever built. He controlled atomic interactions and systematic shifts, used frequency combs and ultrastable lasers, and reached fractional uncertainties near 10^-18. Their clocks have measured the gravitational redshift across height differences at the millimetre scale. They set stringent limits on variation of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark matter, and they motivate a redefinition of the SI second. This is measurement science at its best: noise and systematic errors are beaten down step by step until a new instrument becomes a probe of fundamental physics. Like the SQUID, it turns extraordinary sensitivity into new questions about nature, from relativistic geodesy to searches for new physics.
